Peak Poker Performance

tively, too. We can easily imagine how we will look to our friends and
family if we make a mistake. Our identity can become entangled in
whether or not we are winning or losing. There is a strong need to look
good even if it’s only to ourselves. So, our mind “solves” the problem by
urging us to make the passive play.
   You see, our mind is always giving us direction on what we should do.
Big wins are associated with euphoria and unwarranted confidence. Once
we start feeling good, we’ll often loosen the reigns, because our mind
communicates to us that we can do no wrong. When losses occur, we
may play more cautiously. Or we might go in the opposite direction and
become overly aggressive. Sometimes the mind encourages us to lock up
a win. Many addictions begin as attempts to avoid or get rid of unwanted
thoughts and feelings like boredom, loneliness, anxiety, guilt, anger, or
sadness. The more time and energy we spend trying to get rid of un-
wanted thoughts and feelings, the more likely we are to suffer psycho-
logically in the long run.
   Any strong emotion can significantly influence the way we play. Our
thinking can cause mental blind spots that lead us to make mistakes –
rendering our technical skills useless. Less experienced players tend to be
more emotionally reactive and have less adaptive responses to losing than
more experienced ones.
   We like to think that we are rational, logical creatures, but psychologi-
cal research indicates that this is not the case. We tend to be ruled much
more by emotions than most of us would like to admit. The secret to be-
coming a great poker player is not to get rid of strong emotions but to
keep them from disrupting our analytical decisions.

Emotional Intelligence
When emotions increase to such an extent that we are effectively hijacked,
we lose all semblance of emotional intelligence, a concept popularized by
Daniel Goleman, who defined it as the ability to understand yourself and
others. It is a mental ability and 20 years of research has shown that people
high in emotional intelligence handle stress better and are less likely to en-

                                          Common Psychological Hurdles

gage in self-destructive behaviors. If you are high in emotional intelligence,
you’ll be able to:

   ♠ recognize and assess emotions in yourself and others
   ♠ integrate emotional information into decision making
   ♠ understand the meaning behind your emotions
   ♠ conscientiously manage yourself.

   Basic emotional intelligence skills start with the ability to recognize and
evaluate emotions. You want to be able to identify how you are feeling,
and how emotions affect you physically, and be aware of the thoughts
that are associated with certain emotions. Emotionally intelligent poker
players realize when their emotions are running high and guard against
making errors like those described above. For example, if you recognize
that you’re feeling bored, you can take steps to refresh your energy and
attention. You want to know when you are vulnerable to falling prey to
your emotions. Also, noticing when your opponent is highly emotional can
give you an indication of what mental mistakes they are likely to make.
Then you can use this information to your advantage.
   It is important to notice when your thoughts and emotions are con-
nected to a strong reaction. Typically, strong reactions are not correlated
with sound, competent poker, but are related solely to your internal state.
You must become aware of how you are behaving as you become more
emotional, and it’s critical to understand what is driving your choices. Is
the action you are taking being done to appease your mind, or is it being
done because it’s the most correct action to take given the information
you have? You must shine a light on your issues if you hope to correct
them. If you lack awareness, you’ll remain stuck in losing patterns.

your emotions as they arise. What happens to you physiologically when

   Now that you have had some time to think about your emotional trig-

Mental Game Leaks
Rumination
The first leak is called rumination, which is characterized by negative, re-
petitive, prolonged, unhelpful thinking. Contrast this with constructive
thinking, which is a different state entirely. When we think constructively
we focus on a specific problem, think of potential solutions, and decide to
try something different. When we ruminate, we go over and over previ-
ous difficulties as well as imagined future problems, which can include

                                         Common Psychological Hurdles

how sad we feel or how angry we are. Consider the following common
types of rumination. Are you guilty of:

   ♠ brooding about how bad you have been running
   ♠ stewing on how unfair the situation is
   ♠ replaying bad beats in your mind
   ♠ fantasizing about revenge
   ♠ dwelling on the idea that you are unlucky
   ♠ worrying about what others think about your play
   ♠ telling yourself you are stupid
   ♠ thinking about tilting incidents long after they are over
   ♠ repeatedly going over your mistakes

   The more of these statements you resonate with, the more likely it is
that you are relying on the crutch of rumination. Everyone ruminates from
time to time, but rumination becomes problematic when it impacts your
decision making and focus during the game. The major problem with ru-
minating is that it keeps you focused on the most negative aspects of
your situation and worsens your mood. In turn, this saps your energy and
motivation, and keeps you from taking constructive steps that might ac-
tually improve your game. To top it all off, angry rumination is associated
with high blood pressure, increased heart rate, and muscle tension.
   If you want to get a better handle on rumination, take the time to ac-
quire data on how often and how much you do it. Next time you notice
yourself ruminating, fill out Table 4. If you do this over a period of time,
you’ll start to see patterns in your thinking.

                                          Common Psychological Hurdles

any common themes. Do you tend to ruminate around specific topics or
situations? What are the usual consequences of this behavior? The more
you can learn, the better you’ll understand yourself and the more likely
you’ll be able to replace any unwanted behaviors.
   Here are three quick strategies you can use to stop ruminating:

   ♠ Label it. As soon as you recognize that you’re engaging in
       rumination, label it by saying “this is rumination.” The goal is to
       label your behavior in a non-judgmental way. You are not judging
       yourself for ruminating – your goal is simply to recognize it for
       what it is. You have to recognize that you are engaging in the
       behavior before you can do something more useful.
   ♠ Redirect your attention. Rumination happens when we are not
       fully focused on what we are doing. That’s what gives us the
       opportunity to start thinking unwanted thoughts in the first place.
       As best you can, refocus yourself onto the game by fully attending
       to the action.
   ♠ Choose a constructive behavior. Is there something constructive
       you can do right now to solve your problem or make your situation
       better? If there is, do that instead. Perhaps you can make a few
       notes or text a friend or even your coach. Whatever you do,
       practice getting refocused on the game as quickly as you can.
       Being fully present and focused on the game is a clear antidote to
       rumination.


Avoidance
The next mental game leak to discuss is called avoidance. Most of us have
thoughts, emotions, and memories that we would rather avoid. It seems
sensible, right? If I have tilting thoughts, I should just push them out of my
mind and go on as normal. When we avoid, we work very hard at control-
ling our thoughts and feelings. We do this by taking steps to eliminate, sup-
press, restrain, escape from, or get rid of unwanted thoughts and feelings.

Peak Poker Performance

   There is a paradox, though. The more we try not to think about some-
thing the more we tend to think about it! Let me give you an example.
Don’t think about a white bear. Whatever you do, do not think of a white
bear. Put this book down for the next 10 seconds and whatever you do in
that time, do not think of a white bear.
   So, how did you do? If you are like the majority of people, you were
not able to suppress the image or thought of a white bear. This is one of
the most robust findings in all of cognitive psychology. Harvard professor
Dr. Daniel Wegner is the originator of this little experiment, and time and
time again studies have shown that thought suppression is very difficult
for most people to achieve. Once a concept is evoked in the brain, it is
very difficult to revoke it unless you use very specific, attention grabbing
strategies (which I will share with you in the next chapter).
  The biggest myth in poker is that you should be able to control what
you think and feel. It is a psychological fact that we have much less mas-
tery over what we think and feel than we would like to acknowledge. We
do have some control, but it is a lot less than most of us are probably
comfortable with. It is a basic psychological tenet that we have control
over our actions but not our thoughts and feelings.
    There are countless books and programs that teach that the way to
get rid of negative thoughts is to dispute them and replace them with
positive ones. Such techniques can make you feel better in the short
term, but they usually fail miserably in the long term. The same holds true
for negative emotions like anger, fear, or insecurity. There are a ton of
techniques that you can use to get rid of them temporarily, but they al-
ways seem to return. As long as we are not too stressed or too tilted, we
can usually manage negative thoughts and feelings. Where it gets to be a
problem is when we get very emotional. As our level of distress increases,
our level of control tends to decrease.
    But interestingly enough, a closer look shows that it’s not pain and
stress that cause us difficulties. Trying to escape, control, manage, or get
rid of unwanted thoughts and emotions leads us to lose focus and takes
our attention away from playing. That’s when trouble ensues. Current

                                          Common Psychological Hurdles

peak performance research shows that losing present focus is the main
reason for loss of flow during competitive situations. When we begin to
struggle with unwanted thoughts and emotions, by definition we cannot
be fully focused on what is happening around us.
    Think about what can happen to some players when they lose a hand
they think they should have won. They often get caught in a trap where
they spend their limited time and mental resources ruminating about
what went wrong. They become angry that their opponents “play so bad,”
and may end up feeling sorry for themselves. There’s a tendency to orient
towards a victim mentality. All this adds up to not being able to perform
at your best. As you can clearly see, attempts to mentally control
thoughts can produce a variety of negative consequences.
    The last avoidance strategy is emotional suppression. I want to high-
light this strategy separately just so you get a good sense of it, but know
that it’s very difficult to separate our thoughts and emotions. Most of us
were taught from a young age to “control” our emotions. We heard things
like, “stop feeling sorry for yourself,” “snap out of,” and “get over it.” As a
result, we have learned how to give the appearance of emotional control.
Perhaps you “keep a stiff upper lip” or “put on a brave face” in light of dis-
appointments.
    Even though many of us are trying to control our emotions, rates of de-
pression, anxiety, and addiction are some of the highest they have ever
been, even though as a society we are more advanced than ever. Statistics
show that 30% of the adult population suffers from a diagnosable psychi-
atric disorder in any given year, and by the year 2020 depression will be
the second biggest, most costly, and most debilitating disease in the world.
We also have data showing that almost one out of two people will go
through a stage in life when they seriously consider suicide, and about one
in 10 actually attempt it, at some point. These are sobering statistics espe-
cially when you consider that they don’t include suffering that comes from
things like boredom, loneliness, existential angst, or low self-esteem.
